title: A Parcel Across the River
premise: Play the Sauganash's errand runner on a summer morning in 1835, carrying a traveller's forgotten parcel across the South Branch, deducing which tavern he went to, and deciding how to return.

opening.text:
JAUNT: A PARCEL ACROSS THE RIVER. A summer morning in 1835; you are thirteen, employed to run errands for the Sauganash, the tavern on the east bank of the South Branch. A traveller who lodged here last night has already crossed the river and left his parcel behind. He informed the kitchen which tavern he was heading for, and the kitchen has unfortunately forgotten.

Carry the parcel across the bridge and locate its owner. The town, its taverns and its bridge are historical; the errand runner is invented.

stops.text: The Sauganash stands at the southeast corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east bank of the South Branch. Wau-Bun remembers it as 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters', and in June the Chicago Democrat reported that it had been repaired, refitted and furnished with neatness and taste. The parcel, tied with string, is considerably heavier than it appears. Across the river stand two competing taverns, and the traveller is presumably at one of them, so you will have to deduce which.
stops.narrative: Which establishment: the Green Tree, or Wolf Point?

choices.label: Investigate the Green Tree
choices.consequence: The substantial tavern immediately across the bridge.

choices.label: Investigate Wolf Point
choices.consequence: The older establishment, north at the forks of the river.

stops.text: Across the bridge to the Green Tree, at Lake and West Water. James Kinzie built it in 1833 as the first building in the place erected specifically as a hotel, and Chester Ingersoll is its landlord now. Moses and Kirkland say it was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by'. Now, a surprising future: in 1880 it will be relocated to Milwaukee Avenue, where it will still be standing as 'the oldest memento of early taverns'. Inquire at the door for the traveller, then return to the bridge.
stops.narrative: The hotel named after a neighboring oak.

stops.text: Up to Wolf Point, on the west bank where the North and South Branches meet and flow east to the lake as one river. The tavern here is constructed partly of logs and partly of frame, and Lieutenant Allen fashioned its sign from a piece of a box, painting a wolf on it. Now, a disputed question, since the historical sources disagree: who actually keeps the place? One account says William Walters ran it from 1833 to 1836, while a chronology of the hotels says it stopped operating as a public house in 1834. Ask at the door for the traveller, then return to the bridge.
stops.narrative: The tavern identified by its painted wolf.

stops.text: Back on the South Branch bridge, between Lake and Randolph Streets. The old settlers who used it described log abutments and two bents, about six feet above the water, high enough for teams to pass beneath on the ice. A later history, however, says it 'at first consisted of floating logs tied together', funded by subscription, $486.20, 'of which the Indians of the vicinity contributed $200'. Was it a fixed bridge or a floating one? The accounts directly contradict each other. The parcel has successfully reached its owner. Return directly, or detour to the drawbridge?
stops.narrative: Straight back, or a detour to the drawbridge?

choices.label: Detour to the drawbridge
choices.consequence: A brief inspection of the town's newest bridge.

stops.text: Back at the Sauganash, which Moses and Kirkland call 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its landlord, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'. The parcel has found its owner, your hands are empty, and the morning is not yet half over, yet someone in the kitchen is already calling your name.
stops.narrative: Back at the tavern where the errand originated.

stops.text: East along the river to the foot of Dearborn Street, where the town's first drawbridge spans the main river. Nelson Norton, a ship-carpenter, cut its lumber during the winter of 1833-34 and began construction in March 1834. Andreas says it was 'about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet', built on the 'gallows pattern', with a frame at either end of the draw. Observe it for a minute, then hurry back to the Sauganash before anyone notices that you are missing.

legs.note: West over the South Branch bridge to Lake and West Water.
legs.story: Across the bridge and directly to the corner of Lake and West Water.

legs.note: West over the South Branch bridge and north along the bank to the forks.
legs.story: Across the bridge and north along the riverbank to the forks.

legs.note: Back south along the bank to the bridge.
Over the bridge to the east bank and the Sauganash.
Over the bridge and east along the river to the foot of Dearborn Street.

endings.text: The traveller was at the Green Tree, exactly as you guessed, and he gave you a penny for returning his parcel. You ran straight back across the bridge, where the Sauganash kitchen had three additional errands waiting.

The traveller was at the Green Tree, and the parcel is his again. Then you stole a few minutes to watch the drawbridge, and the Sauganash kitchen immediately noticed your absence. Next time, return immediately.
Wolf Point was the correct guess: the traveller was there and grateful for his parcel. You hurried back across the bridge and completed the morning's remaining errands before noon.

The traveller was at Wolf Point, and the parcel is his again. On the way home you stopped to observe the drawbridge considerably longer than you intended, and the Sauganash kitchen has been calling for you for an hour.

keepsake.title: A Parcel Delivered
keepsake.text: A made-up errand slip from the Sauganash in the summer of 1835: which tavern you tried, and which way you came home. No real traveller, parcel or errand runner is written on it.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun describes the Sauganash in 1831 as 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters'.
evidence.locator: Ch. XVII, 'Chicago in 1831' — the Wolf Point houses, Mark Beaubien's house just completed.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town's public houses (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Sauganash stood at the south-east corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east bank of the South Branch.
evidence.reasoning: The corner is given by the hotel chronology and the Chicago Landmark designation; the building's coordinate in the scene is the structure record's platted-corner derivation and carries the georeference's uncertainty of about 20 m.

evidence.text: The Green Tree was a public house at Lake and West Water; the old settlers' account gives Chester Ingersoll as its landlord from 1834 to 1837.
evidence.locator: Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883, 'Old Chicago' early-hotels feature as transcribed by Chicagology; landlord chronology (Ingersoll, 1834–1837).

evidence.text: James Kinzie built the Green Tree in 1833 as the first building in the place erected for hotel purposes; Chester Ingersoll is given as landlord 1834–1837.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 127, Green Tree Tavern: construction and landlords; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Green Tree entry.

evidence.text: The Green Tree was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by', 'one of the most noted in those early days'; it stood until 1880, when it was moved to 33-37 Milwaukee Avenue, 'where it still stands, the oldest memento of early taverns'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree's corner is on the west bank of the South Branch, with the river to its east.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record places the tavern at the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, its river end on the bank (position inferred, moved on the owner's ruling T-0141); West Water Street is the west-bank frontage, so the river lies east of it.

evidence.text: Wentworth's tavern at the Point was partly log and partly frame, on the ground north of the Lake Street crossing; Lieutenant Allen made its sign from a piece of a box and painted a picture of a wolf on it.
evidence.locator: Chicagology, 'Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago': the forks buildings sentence ('partly log and partly frame'), and the note at the page's foot on Wentworth's sign ('He painted a picture of a wolf on it').

evidence.text: One account has William Walters keeping the tavern from 1833 to 1836; the hotel chronology says it ceased operations as a public house in 1834.
evidence.locator: DRLOIH, 'The Beginning of Wolf Point', the tavern's operator succession (Walters 1833–1836); DRLOIH hotel chronology, Wolf Point Tavern entry ('ceased operations as a public house in 1834').

evidence.text: The tavern stood on the west bank at the forks, where the North and South Branches meet and run east to the lake as one river.
evidence.reasoning: DRLOIH puts the tavern 'on the west bank of the river at Wolf Point' and Wau-Bun's 1831 sequence has it 'facing down the river from the west'. That Wolf Point is the confluence is read from the project's committed river trace (the datum origin is the forks), not stated in either sentence. The building's exact distance north of Lake Street is not fixed by any source.

evidence.text: Old settlers' statement on the first bridges over the branches: both were built on log abutments and two bents, about ten feet wide, and about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice.
evidence.locator: Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1, footnote across pp. 631–632, signed J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble (1883).

evidence.text: The bridge across the South Branch near Randolph Street 'at first consisted of floating logs tied together'; Alanson H. and Charles Taylor built it from funds raised by subscription, $486.20, 'of which the Indians of the vicinity contributed $200'.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12185-12192 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Later retellings call the South Branch crossing a log raft bridge; the settlers' statement of abutments, bents and clearance describes a fixed bridge, and the record adopts the fixed reading while keeping the name.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record's research note holds the conflict open: a floating raft has no abutments, no bents resting on the bottom and no six feet of air beneath it, so four men who used the bridge are preferred over the retold type-word.

evidence.text: The bridge crossed the South Branch between Lake and Randolph Streets, its west landing on West Water Street; the exact station along that reach is placed at the midpoint because the accounts pull opposite ways.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record places the deck at the midpoint of the 69 m reach between Lake and Randolph, between the traced 1834 waterlines; its documented range runs from 1833 to an attestation of 18 August 1835, so it stands on the scene date.

evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland call the Sauganash 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its genial landlord, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'.
evidence.locator: p. 87, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 11879-11886 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Nelson R. Norton, a ship-carpenter, writes in a letter Andreas prints that he cut the lumber for a drawbridge over the winter of 1833-34 and began building it in March 1834; Andreas notes the Democrat has it formally accepted by the Trustees in August. It was the first drawbridge across the river.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the bridges section, Norton's letter beginning 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833' and Andreas's correction 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge'; with 'The first drawbridge thrown across the river was at Dearborn Street'. Read in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.

evidence.text: Andreas: 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' It was of the 'gallows pattern', with frames one at either end of the draw.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 415 (per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4), the paragraph on the Dearborn Street drawbridge, read verbatim in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.

evidence.text: The bridge crosses the main stem in line with Dearborn Street, its south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record dearborn_street_drawbridge, which places the crossing on the street it is named for and grades the position inferred. The jaunt starts at the south end; the crossing is the route's and claims no dated passage over the draw.

evidence.text: The errand runner the visitor plays, their age and work at the Sauganash, the traveller, his parcel and his penny, the guess at which tavern he went to, the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Parcel Delivered keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such runner, traveller or parcel is recorded; no named person is met or speaks, and the walk stays on a summer morning of 1835.
